entry.title: Curl Accidentally Turing-Complete for Nine Months
entry.content:
Links: seriot.ch | discussion | hacker news

Between versions 8.12 and 8.16, the command-line data transfer tool curl possessed features that made it accidentally Turing-complete under unbounded resource assumptions. Config files could slice variable values and recursively include other files without an explicit depth cap, enabling the utility to simulate any two-counter Minsky program.

Release 8.17.0 introduced a five-level include cap that broke this reduction by restricting file inclusion depth. Although real-world physical constraints such as stack limits and memory allocation restricted execution depth in practice, the behavior illustrated how unexpected computational capabilities can emerge from configuration parsers.

While subsequent pre-releases resolved the vast majority of these bugs, the default optimistic concurrency control mode continued to experience data loss on committed writes, and the strictest serializable settings still allowed concurrency anomalies.

entry.title: Mozilla Details Strategy to Defend Firefox Against Automated Patch-Gapping
entry.content:
Links: blog.mozilla.org | discussion

Mozilla is adapting Firefox's security practices to counter patch-gapping, a vulnerability exploitation method accelerated by AI models that can rapidly reverse-engineer software security fixes. While frontier models have enabled the Firefox team to significantly increase its security fix rate, malicious actors are increasingly using automated tools to target the brief window of time between a code fix and full user deployment.

To neutralize this threat regardless of attack speed, Firefox is introducing a structural defense that staggers fixes across independent sandbox layers so that interdependent vulnerabilities do not share overlapping patch gaps. Additionally, the browser team is accelerating its release cycle, withholding regression tests until fixes are shipped, and scanning new code commits to maintain a security advantage over automated attackers.

entry.title: Go 1.28 HTTP/2 Parking Mechanism Reduces Server Memory Usage
entry.content:
Links: abdolirad.me | discussion | hacker news

An analysis of the draft Go 1.28 release notes examines a new HTTP/2 server mechanism called parking, which allows connection-serving goroutines to exit when there is no active work instead of waiting idle. Benchmarks comparing a Go 1.28 development build with parking enabled versus disabled show that handling 5,000 idle HTTP/2 connections results in 5,000 fewer active goroutines and a resident set size (RSS) reduction of roughly 85 to 93 MiB.

The benchmark results indicate that enabling parking lowers stack memory usage by approximately 78 MiB under the same load, while heap allocation metrics remain variable across test runs. Because the feature is evaluated on a pre-release development build using an experimental and temporary debug setting, the findings highlight potential memory efficiency gains for servers maintaining thousands of idle connections rather than guaranteed outcomes for all workloads.

entry.content:

Researchers at University College London have found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives survived the asteroid impact 66 million years ago largely due to a long-standing preference for warm environments. By analyzing more than 7,000 fossils alongside computer climate models spanning 245 million years, the team determined that equatorial regions remained climatically suitable for these animals while habitats for non-avian dinosaurs sharply contracted.

The study, published in Science Advances, highlights that the broader crocodile lineage historically tracked warm conditions by expanding ranges during hot periods and retreating toward the tropics during cooling phases. The authors note that while this behavioral consistency helped them endure past mass extinctions, modern pressures such as habitat fragmentation and urbanization may restrict the ability of contemporary species to shift ranges in response to current climate change.

Sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest burden, accounting for 45% of global envenomings and fatalities, with rates nearly three times higher than those in south Asia. The findings also show that over 800,000 survivors suffer long-term physical disabilities annually, exacerbating poverty in vulnerable rural communities and underscoring the need for targeted antivenom stockpiling and improved healthcare access to meet World Health Organization reduction targets.

entry.title: Redox OS Details Ring Buffers Implementation and Performance Improvements
entry.content:
Links: redox-os.org | discussion

The Redox OS team has concluded a grant-funded project supported by the NLnet Foundation to implement io_uring-like ring buffer support at the system task level. The new redox-rings crate and associated FFI API allow applications to asynchronously submit I/O requests and communicate with system daemons like RamFS and NVMed via shared memory without kernel involvement or data copying.

Alongside the ring buffer machinery and a new async driver executor, the team implemented several kernel and IPC optimizations—such as direct context switching, vector register zeroing on syscall paths, and 2MB huge page support—which collectively reduced IPC roundtrip latency and accelerated benchmark performance significantly.

entry.title: V12 Research Reveals Weak AES-256 Key Generation in Multiple PDF Implementations
entry.content:
Links: v12.sh | discussion | hacker news

Security researchers at V12 discovered that several popular PDF implementations generate AES-256 file keys from insufficiently random sources or excessively small state spaces, enabling attackers to decrypt protected documents without a password. In affected applications, the cryptographic keys are derived from predictable metrics rather than true random entropy.

Specifically, MuPDF's reliance on a linear congruential generator limits the effective entropy of its keys to just nine bits, making rapid brute-force recovery feasible within milliseconds. Similar predictable key derivation patterns were identified in Foxit and Java-based libraries like OpenPDF and iText, undermining the security guarantees of AES-256 encryption in previously generated files.

entry.title: Qwenputer Embeds RISC-V CPU into Qwen 3.5 Weights
entry.content:

Qwenputer is an experimental model based on Qwen 3.5 4B that embeds a 32-bit RISC-V CPU directly into its weights. By using Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers as exact, addressable RAM, the CPU executes arithmetic, C, and MicroPython code during forward passes without external runtimes or tool calls.

The implementation uses one-hot key encoding for memory access and has achieved 100% accuracy on specific long-integer arithmetic benchmarks. An experimental filesystem also allows the model to store and retrieve text data via the DeltaNet state, providing persistent memory across conversation sessions.
